 | 5 | `Expanded` |
 | 6 | `Busy` |
 
 `STATE` is a **semantic/accessibility** property the application sets; it never
 describes visual styling (hover/press styles stay renderer/token-owned).
 
 `STRING` properties carry their text in the frame's string section: the
 property value is the *relative* offset of a length-prefixed entry, exactly as
 `SET_TEXT`'s `B` field does.
 
 `TOGGLE` (`0x24`) is a boolean control whose visual style is a **token**, not a
 separate component: `TOGGLE_STYLE` (`0x2018`, ENUM) selects the native variant —
 `Switch` (sliding pill), `Checkbox` (square with checkmark), or `Button`
 (toggle button). The checked state is `SELECTED` (`0x2004`, U8 0/1), emitted
 guest → host and reported back host → guest. The renderer owns the visual
 presentation (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)).
 
 `SLIDER` (`0x25`) is a continuous numeric control: the guest emits its
 `VALUE` plus the `MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE` range, and the renderer reports value
 changes back as `VALUE_CHANGED` events (host → guest), resolving the semantic
 value from its own track geometry (see [EVENT](#event-0x03--host--guest)).
 
 ### EVENT (0x03) — host → guest
 
 The event commands and their `EVENT_LISTENERS` bits are catalogued in
 [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) (core events, SwiftUI-style); this file defines the
 wire encoding.
 
 Events are the **raw inputs**: the renderer reports what happened (a pointer
 went down/moved/up, a key went down/up) and resolves which node it hit via its
 own rendered-output tree. High-level interpretations — tap, drag, long-press —
 are built by the guest/app from these raw inputs and are **not** part of the
 protocol.
 
 #### Event listeners (which nodes emit events)
 
 A renderer reports raw events only for nodes that declared they want them. The
 application declares this intent through the `EVENT_LISTENERS` semantic
 property (`0x2005`, a u32 bitmask, `SET_PROPERTY` with the `U32` value type).
 Each bit requests a raw-input event kind (see [`listener`] flags):
 
 | Bit | Mask | Event command | Meaning |
 |-----|------|---------------|---------|
 | 0 | `0x00000001` | `POINTER_DOWN` | Report pointer-down for this node |
 | 1 | `0x00000002` | `POINTER_MOVE` | Report pointer-move/enter/leave |
 | 2 | `0x00000004` | `POINTER_UP` | Report pointer-up for this node |
 | 3 | `0x00000008` | `KEY_DOWN` | Report key-down |
 | 4 | `0x00000010` | `KEY_UP` | Report key-up |
 
 > Bits 5–9 (draft) are allocated in [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md#event-listeners-event_listeners)
 > for `FOCUS_CHANGED`, `EDITING_CHANGED`, `SUBMIT`, `SCROLL`, and `WHEEL`.
 > Value-bearing controls (`SLIDER`, `TOGGLE`, `DATE_PICKER`, …) report their
 > value changes by component type and do not need a listener bit.
 
 This is what makes **any element** (a `Text`, a `VStack`, …) able to emit
 events — the renderer attaches native input recognition to the matching native
 element when the listener bit is set, not only to buttons. A renderer SHOULD
 report `POINTER_DOWN`/`POINTER_UP` for a node with the `POINTER_DOWN`/
 `POINTER_UP` bits set by attaching a native click/press gesture to that
 element.
 
 | Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags | Description |
 |---------|-------|---|---|---|-------|-------------|
 | `POINTER_DOWN` | `0x01` | targetId | x (f32) | y (f32) | `POINTER_SECONDARY` | Pointer button pressed at viewport-relative point |
 | `POINTER_MOVE` | `0x02` | targetId | x (f32) | y (f32) | `HOVER_ENTER` / `HOVER_LEAVE` | Pointer moved (bit 0 = entered/hovering, bit 1 = leaving) |
 | `POINTER_UP` | `0x03` | targetId | x (f32) | y (f32) | `POINTER_SECONDARY` | Pointer button released at viewport-relative point |
 | `KEY_DOWN` | `0x04` | targetId | keyCode (u16, low) | modifiers (u8, low) | `KEY_REPEAT` | Key pressed (bit 1 = auto-repeat) |
 | `KEY_UP` | `0x05` | targetId | keyCode (u16, low) | modifiers (u8, low) | — | Key released |
 | `VALUE_CHANGED` | `0x06` | targetId | value (f32) | 0 | — | A value-bearing control changed (e.g. slider); the renderer resolves the semantic value from its track geometry |
 | `TEXT_CHANGED` | `0x07` | targetId | string offset | 0 | — | A text field's value changed; the new text is a length-prefixed entry in the **event arena** (shared memory, absolute `B` offset) or the batch's string section (network, *relative* `B` offset) — the same dual convention as `PARAMETER::SET_TEXT` |
 | `NAVIGATE` | `0x0E` | 0 | URL string offset | 0 | `NAVIGATE_URL` | Global navigation request: with the flag, `B` is the destination URL (browser `popstate`/back/forward/deep-link, same dual string convention as `TEXT_CHANGED`); without the flag, "back one step" (native back affordance). Never node-keyed, never `EVENT_LISTENERS`-gated — see [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md#navigation) |
 
 ### META (0x04)
 
 | Command | Value | A | B | C | Description |
 |---------|-------|---|---|---|-------------|
 | `RESET` | `0x01` | 0 | 0 | 0 | Host must clear all rendered output |
 | `ENVIRONMENT` | `0x02` | fieldId (u16, low) | field value | 0 | A platform environment field (host → guest) — see [Environment fields](#environment-fields) |
 | `RESYNC` | `0x03` | 0 | 0 | 0 | The host (renderer) requests a **full snapshot** of the current tree (host → guest). The guest answers with a single full-snapshot batch (the same TREE + PARAMETER stream as a mount). Used for reconnect/gap recovery and no-JS refresh. |
 | `PING` | `0x04` | 0 | 0 | 0 | A transport-liveness **heartbeat probe** (guest → host). No payload. **Network batch transport only** — a shared-memory ring consumer MUST NOT expect, emit, or relay it. See [Transport heartbeat](#transport-heartbeat). |

The renderer re-resolves every token-referencing property; while forced, platform scheme changes are ignored. See [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md#color-schemes-light--dark). |
 | `RESET_THEME` | `0x07` | 0 | 0 | 0 | **Draft.** Clear every application design-token override (base + `dark.*`) and re-resolve against renderer defaults (guest → host). Emit before a replacement theme's `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` opcodes in the same frame. |
 | `SET_WINDOW_METADATA` | `0x08` | fieldId (u16, low) | field value | 0 | **Draft.** Presentation metadata for the host window/surface that owns the stream (guest → host) — see [Window metadata](#window-metadata). |
 
 #### Environment fields
 
 `META::ENVIRONMENT` is an **extensible field family** (mirroring
 `PARAMETER::SET_PROPERTY`): each opcode sets one platform environment field, so
 any number of fields ride one batch and new fields are new ids — never new
 commands. The platform (renderer / DOM client / SSR host) delivers the
 application's launch context this way; an HTTP request supplies what it offers,
 and the WebSocket connection **enriches** the environment after connect
 (viewport, native deep-links, and future fields all arrive the same way).
 
 | Field | Value | `B` encoding | Notes |
 |-------|-------|--------------|-------|
 | `VIEWPORT_WIDTH` | `0x0001` | f32 | Logical points |
 | `VIEWPORT_HEIGHT` | `0x0002` | f32 | Logical points |
 | `ROUTE` | `0x0003` | string offset | The initial route/deep-link path. String convention is the `TEXT_CHANGED`/`NAVIGATE` dual: absolute offset into the host → guest **event arena** over the shared ring, *relative* offset into the batch's string section over the network. |
 
 **Delivery** (spec DSL.md §4.5): on SSR the host synthesizes the environment
 from the HTTP request (`ROUTE` = request path — all the request offers); over
 the WebSocket the DOM client sends it (viewport + `ROUTE`) as its first message;
 a reconnect re-sends it. The application applies the environment uniformly — the
 router hydrates from the `ROUTE` field before mount, so a deep-link renders
 correctly on the first frame.
 
 #### Window metadata
 
 `META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA` is an **extensible field family** for presentation
 metadata of the host **window/surface** that owns the stream (a browser tab, a
 native window, an embedded surface). One opcode sets one field; new fields are
 new ids, never new commands. The protocol defines the concept; **each renderer
 maps it onto its own chrome** — the browser mapping is only one of them:
 
 | Renderer | `TITLE` | `DESCRIPTION` | `LOCALE` |
 |----------|---------|---------------|----------|
 | HTML / SSR | `<title>` | `<meta name="description">` | `<html lang>` |
 | DOM client | `document.title` | meta description | `<html lang>` |
 | GTK4 | window/headerbar title | accessible description | — |
 | Qt | window title | — | — |
 
 | Field | Value | `B` encoding | Notes |
 |-------|-------|--------------|-------|
 | `TITLE` | `0x0001` | string offset | Title of the hosting window/surface |
 | `DESCRIPTION` | `0x0002` | string offset | Human-readable description of the current content |
 | `LOCALE` | `0x0003` | string offset | BCP 47 content locale |
 
 The string encoding follows the same convention as `SET_TEXT`/`ROUTE`: an
 absolute offset into the guest arena over the shared ring, or a *relative*
 offset into the batch's string section over the network. An **empty string
 clears** the field, and the renderer applies its own default. Metadata is
 renderer-global (not part of the retained tree), survives `META::RESET`, and is
 re-emitted in a full snapshot (`META::RESYNC`).
 
 Semantics:
 
 - The application owns the values; a bound signal change emits exactly the
   changed field (like a property diff).
 - A proxied origin's window metadata is **ignored** — an embedded app never
   retitles the host window (spec/PROXY.md).
 - Web-only artifacts (`canonical`, `robots`, sitemap) are host concerns and are
-  **not** protocol fields.
+  **not** protocol fields. A web renderer may accept them (plus Open
+  Graph/Twitter/JSON-LD) as an **out-of-band render option** for one render
+  call; this is renderer input, never guest state.
 
 ---
 
 ## Reactive Emission
 
 The engine emits **only what changed** relative to its previous emission:
 
 - **Property diff**: a changed `spacing`/`padding`/`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`ALIGNMENT`/
   text emits a single `SET_PROPERTY` / `SET_TEXT` for that node. (Padding is a
   styling modifier, but it still diffs and emits like any other property.)
 - **Structural diff**: a node added/removed/moved emits the corresponding
   `TREE` opcode(s).
 - **Steady state**: an unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes.
 
 The **`frame` compound modifier** (width/height/alignment) is not a distinct
 protocol concept: it emits `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`ALIGNMENT` as ordinary
 `PARAMETER:SET_PROPERTY` deltas, exactly like any other constraint property. There
 is no `frame` opcode or dedicated wire type.
 
 Signals in the application drive this: a signal marks the tree dirty; the
 engine's next `emit` reconciles and writes only the delta. The renderer applies
 each frame as a delta to its native elements.
 
 ---
 
 ## Linear Memory Layout
 
 The guest engine and host share a **single linear memory**. Regions are fixed at module start:
 
 ```
 +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
 | 0x0000  Header block (80 B)  — cursors, frame counter, layout  |
 | 0x0050  Ring buffer (16 B × slotCount)   [guest → host]        |
 | ...      (slots densely packed, 64-byte aligned base)          |
 | 0x10050 Event ring buffer (16 B × slotCount) [host → guest]    |
 | ...                                                           |
 | 0x20050 Arena (bump region, guest-owned: strings / tokens)     |
 | ...                                                           |
 | 0x30050 Event arena (bump region, host-owned: event strings)   |
 | ...                                                            |
 +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
 ```
 
 > The event ring is the **host → guest** direction of the shared-memory
 > transport: the renderer writes `EVENT`-category opcodes here and the
 > guest/app drains them. It uses the same 16-byte slot layout as the main
 > (guest → host) ring; both share `slotCount` (same capacity).
 >
 > The **event arena** is the host-owned bump region that makes strings flow
 > **host → guest** over the shared ring: a renderer bump-allocates `TEXT_CHANGED`
 > text (and any future string-bearing event payload) here and references it by
 > its absolute byte offset — exactly mirroring how the guest uses the guest
 > arena for `SET_TEXT` / STRING properties. The host resets its cursor on
 > `META::RESET`; if the event arena is full the host applies backpressure
 > (drops/stalls the event), mirroring ring backpressure.
 
 ### Header block (80 bytes)
 
 | Offset | Size | Field | Producer | Description |
 |--------|------|-------|----------|-------------|
 | 0x00 | 4 | `magic` | — | `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`) |
 | 0x04 | 2 | `version` | — | Wire protocol version (1) |
 | 0x06 | 4 | `ringOffset` | — | Byte offset of the ring region |
 | 0x0A | 4 | `ringBytes` | — | Byte length of the ring region |
 | 0x0E | 4 | `slotCount` | — | Number of ring slots (power of two) |
 | 0x12 | 4 | `arenaOffset` | — | Byte offset of the arena region |
 | 0x16 | 4 | `arenaBytes` | — | Byte length of the arena region |
 | 0x1A | 4 | `arenaCursor` | guest | Next free byte in the arena |
 | 0x1E | 4 | `readCursor` | host | Ring slot the host has consumed up to |
 | 0x22 | 4 | `writeCursor` | guest | Ring slot the guest has written up to |
 | 0x26 | 4 | `frameCount` | guest | Monotonic completed-frame counter |
 | 0x2A | 4 | `eventRingOffset` | — | Byte offset of the host→guest event ring region |
 | 0x2E | 4 | `eventRingBytes` | — | Byte length of the event ring region |
 | 0x32 | 4 | `eventSlotCount` | — | Event ring slot count (power of two; = `slotCount`) |
 | 0x36 | 4 | `eventReadCursor` | guest | Event ring slot the guest has consumed up to |
 | 0x3A | 4 | `eventWriteCursor` | host | Event ring slot the host has written up to |
 | 0x40 | 4 | `eventArenaOffset` | — | Byte offset of the host→guest event arena region |
 | 0x44 | 4 | `eventArenaBytes` | — | Byte length of the event arena region |
 | 0x48 | 4 | `eventArenaCursor` | host | Next free byte in the event arena |
 
 ### Ring buffer
 
 - Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
 - **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
 - **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
 - **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
 - **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.
 
 ### Event ring (host → guest)
 
 - The **host** (renderer) is the producer: it writes `EVENT`-category opcodes at `eventWriteCursor`.
 - The **guest** (app/engine) is the consumer: it reads from `eventReadCursor` up to `eventWriteCursor`, then advances `eventReadCursor`.
 - Events are raw inputs and are consumed as soon as they are written (no frame batching); `eventFrameCount` is not required.
 - Backpressure mirrors the main ring: the host must not advance `eventWriteCursor` past `eventReadCursor`.
 
 ### Arena
 
 - A pre-allocated **bump region** for variable-length data (strings, token paths).
 - Every arena entry is **self-describing**: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`.
 - Opcodes reference entries by their **byte offset** (`arenaRef`), so an entry's length is read directly from the arena — all opcodes stay 16 bytes.
 - The guest advances `arenaCursor` monotonically (no free-list, no fragmentation). The arena MAY be reset via `META::RESET`.
 
 ### Event arena (host → guest)
 
 The event arena is the **host-owned mirror** of the arena, giving the shared-memory
 transport a host → guest string section so strings flow **both ways on all
 transports**:
 
 - The **host** (renderer) bump-allocates event string payloads here (e.g. the
   new text of a `TEXT_CHANGED`) and references them by their **absolute byte
   offset** in the event opcode — the same `SET_TEXT` shared-memory convention
   used in the guest arena.
 - The **guest** resolves the text from the event arena region when draining
   events (`EVENT::TEXT_CHANGED`).
 - Entries share the same self-describing `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]` layout as
   the guest arena.
 - The host advances `eventArenaCursor` monotonically and resets it on
   `META::RESET`; a full event arena is backpressure (the host drops/stalls the
   event until the guest drains or a reset lands).
 - Over the **network**, host → guest string payloads use the batch's string
   section with *relative* offsets instead (see [Transport](#transport)) — the
   same dual absolute/relative convention as `SET_TEXT`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Colors
 
 Literal colors are **sRGB** (IEC 61966-2-1, D65 white point), packed as `0xAARRGGBB`:
 
 - `AA`: alpha (0x00 transparent – 0xFF opaque)
 - `RR`: red, `GG`: green, `BB`: blue
 
 Stored little-endian in a `u32` payload. A color **property** may alternatively carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path instead of a literal (see [Design Token System](#design-token-system)); semantic token resolution and theme adaptation remain **renderer-owned**.
 
 ---
 
 ## Design Token System
 
 ### Core Principle
 
 > **The application owns the theme. The renderer owns the defaults, the scheme
 > detection, and the interaction states.**
 
 - The **application** declares a theme: token overrides (base = **light**
   design, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark** design) and token references in style
   properties.
 - The **renderer** supplies platform-appropriate defaults, derives the
   effective color scheme from the platform, resolves token references, and
   owns hover/pressed/focus/disabled styling.
 
 This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency
 when the application rolls a theme.
 
 ### Tokens & color schemes
 
 - Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (`color.primary`,
   `font.body.size`, `space.2`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The
   `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the
   arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.
 - **Base = light. `dark.`-prefixed paths are the dark variant** (`dark.color.primary`).
   The renderer derives the effective scheme (light/dark) from the platform and
   re-resolves when it changes. An application MAY force a scheme with
   `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` (platform/light/dark); the override is renderer-wide
   and `platform` restores native detection. A `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose
   path starts with `dark.` always resolves against the dark layer, regardless
   of the active scheme (an explicit dark-variant reference).
 - The **standard token catalog** (colors, typography, spacing, radii,
   elevations, `control.*`, per-component tokens) and the **resolution
   algorithm** (dark layer → override → default → parent → fallback) are defined
   in **[TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md)**.
 
 ### References in properties
 
 Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY instead
 carry the **`DESIGN_TOKEN`** value type (`0x08`), with `C` = arenaRef to the
 token path. The renderer resolves the reference against the token tables and the
 current scheme. A property carries exactly one value — a literal or a token
 reference, never both. Because overrides and the scheme are renderer state, a
 token-typed property requires **no re-emission** when a token changes. A
 `dark.`-prefixed reference resolves the dark layer regardless of the active
 scheme; an unresolvable reference leaves the property unset (renderer default).
 
 ### Renderer Responsibilities
 
 The renderer MUST:
 
 1. Provide platform-appropriate **light and dark defaults** for all Tier 1 tokens.
 2. Accept `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides.
 3. Derive the effective color scheme from the platform and re-resolve on change.
 4. Resolve token references (`DESIGN_TOKEN` value type) in properties.
 5. Fall back to defaults when no override exists.
 6. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.
 
 The application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (base and `dark.*`)
 and reference tokens via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type; it MUST NOT assume
 specific default token values. Tokens a renderer cannot apply are ignored (the
 same "allowed and ignored" rule as unapplicable modifiers).
 
 ---
 
 ## Frame Lifecycle
 
 A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:
 
 1. Guest begins a frame.
 2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
 3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
 4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
 5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.
 
 Because the ring and arena are plain memory, the guest publishes via a single release store of `frameCount`; the host acquires on read.
 
 > **Unique node-id invariant.** A frame MUST NOT contain two nodes with the same
 > id. `TREE` and `PARAMETER` opcodes reference each node id for exactly one node,
 > so every id-keyed consumer (the renderer's `id → element` map, `PLAYBACK_STATE`,
 > `MEDIA_*`, proxy remapping, …) stays unambiguous. A full-snapshot emission of a
 > subtree materialized more than once (e.g. a `SIZE_THAT_FITS` candidate shared
 > between branches, spec/PRIMITIVES.md §SizeThatFits) MUST give **every copy a
 > distinct id** — no id is reused between copies, including identity-stable nodes.
 
 ---
 
 ## Transport
 
 The opcode protocol is transport-agnostic. Two peer backends carry frames from
 producer (guest engine) to consumer (host renderer):
 
 | Backend | Scenario | Mechanism |
 |---------|----------|-----------|
 | Shared memory | Desktop / native (guest + host share linear memory) | The ring buffer + arena above; zero-copy |
 | Network batch | SSR → browser (guest and host do **not** share memory) | Serialized batches of opcodes + arena delta |
 
 The `Frame` type is the **transport seam**: a consumer (renderer) applies a
 frame the same way whether it came from the shared-memory ring or a decoded
 network batch.
 
 ### Network batch format
 
 ```
 [u32 magic "PLPL"] [u16 version] [u16 flags] [u32 sequence] [u32 opcodeCount]
 [opcode × opcodeCount (16 B each)]
 [u32 arenaDeltaLen] [arena delta bytes]
 ```
 
 - **magic / version**: `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`, little-endian on the wire) / `1`.
   A decoder MUST reject batches with a mismatched magic or version.
 - **flags**: direction. `0x0000` = guest → host (tree/style). Bit `0x0001` =
   host → guest (raw-input events); host → guest batches carry their string
   payloads in the batch's string section.
 - **sequence**: a **per-stream monotonic message sequence** — the producer
   increments it by exactly one for each batch it encodes (guest → host delta
   batches only; heartbeat/request batches carry `0`). It is the network
   transport's loss detector; see [Sequence gap detection](#sequence-gap-detection).
   It is **not** the ring header's `frameCount` (a per-frame publish watermark
   for shared memory): opcodes from several emit-pass frames may coalesce into
   one batch, so a batch is the network unit, not a frame.
 - **arena delta**: the bytes appended to the bump arena since the previous
   batch. The consumer keeps a **mirrored arena** and appends each delta, so
   absolute `arenaRef` offsets stay valid — identical to shared memory.
 - **META::RESET**: a batch containing a reset opcode clears the consumer's
   mirrored arena before appending (offsets restart at 0).
 
 ### Batching policy
 
 The producer buffers opcodes and flushes a batch when **either** threshold is
 reached (first trigger wins):
 
 - **Time**: the interval since the first buffered opcode elapses (default **4 ms**).
 - **Size**: the accumulated batch reaches a network-frame size (default **1400 bytes**).
 
 Both thresholds are configurable; a producer MAY flush eagerly (e.g. on the
 first frame after connection).
 
 ### Sequence gap detection
 
 The network backend is reliable and ordered **within a connection**, but a
 middlebox can drop a batch while the socket stays "open", and a producer's send
 path can wedge — either way the consumer silently misses deltas. The batch
 `sequence` makes that loss detectable:
 
 - **Producer**: maintain one monotonic `sequence` per stream, incremented by
   exactly one for **each encoded batch**. Only guest → host delta batches
   consume a sequence number; heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) and request
   batches (`META::RESYNC`, `META::ENVIRONMENT`, events) carry `0` and never
   advance it.
 - **Consumer**: the first guest → host batch establishes a baseline
   (`expected = sequence + 1`). Every later guest → host batch MUST satisfy
   `sequence == expected`; then `expected = sequence + 1`. A batch whose
   sequence does not match means one or more batches were lost.
 - **Recovery**: on a gap the consumer MUST NOT apply the gapped batch (its
   deltas assume the lost state) and MUST request a full snapshot
   (`META::RESYNC`), then re-baseline on the next guest → host batch. The
   consumer also re-baselines on every (re)connect.
 - **Heartbeat batches are exempt**: a `META::PONG` (host → guest) is not part of
   the guest → host stream; consumers track only guest → host batches.
 
 The recovery is **always a full snapshot**, never retransmission: the renderer
 is stateless and the application owns the retained tree, so a `META::RESYNC`
 reconverges the consumer regardless of what was lost. **Acknowledgements and a
 retransmit queue are deliberately not part of the protocol** — they would add a
 per-session send buffer and an ack exchange to a design whose recovery is
 already a stateless snapshot.
 
 ### Transport heartbeat
 
 The **network batch backend** (a WebSocket / streamed connection) can fail
 silently: a proxy or load balancer may drop the connection without a close
 frame, or the peer's send path may wedge, leaving the socket "open" while
 nothing is delivered. Neither side can detect this from the batch stream alone.
 The heartbeat is the transport-liveness mechanism for this backend:
 
 - **Probe**: the guest (client) sends a `META::PING` batch at a fixed cadence
   (default **every 5 s**). `A/B/C = 0`, no string section.
 - **Reply**: the host (server) MUST answer each `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
   batch as promptly as its send path allows.
 - **Liveness**: a peer's *liveness* is any received batch — deltas, `PONG`, or
   anything else. A guest that receives no batch for **more than two probe
   intervals** SHOULD treat the connection as dead: close it and reconnect (the
   reconnect flow already re-syncs via `META::RESYNC`).
 - **Host-side detection**: a host MAY additionally send WebSocket-protocol-level
   ping frames (browsers auto-answer) to detect a dead client and keep
   middleboxes from timing the connection out; a host whose send fails (or a
   probe that is never answered) SHOULD close the connection so the client
   reconnects instead of stalling.
 - **Scope**: the heartbeat is **transport liveness only, NOT app state**. A
   `META::PING`/`META::PONG` batch MUST NOT be routed into the application — it
   never touches the retained tree, signals, or events. The **shared-memory ring
   backend MUST NOT use it**: ring peers are co-located and their liveness is the
   host process's concern, so the ring never carries, expects, or relays
   `META::PING`/`META::PONG`.
 
 ---
 
 ## Conformance
 
 Golden byte vectors for this protocol are in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md).
 
 ### Companion specifications
 
 The protocol's semantic surface is catalogued in five companion documents:
 [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md) (the primitive views), [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md)
 (the core modifiers, i.e. the `PARAMETER` properties), [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md)
 (the core events, i.e. the raw inputs), [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md) (the design
 tokens / theming contract), and [ICONS.md](./ICONS.md) (the canonical icon
 vocabulary for the `ICON` primitive). IDs are allocated there spec-first;
 this file remains the wire-format authority and must be updated when new IDs
 land.
 
 > **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
 > in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. This document
 > defines the protocol contract only.

pub(crate) fn resolve_url(canonical: Option<&str>, src: &str) -> String {
    if src.is_empty() { return String::new(); }
    if src.starts_with("http://") || src.starts_with("https://") || src.starts_with("//") { return src.to_string(); }
    if let Some(c) = canonical {
        if src.starts_with('/') {
            if let Some(origin) = origin_of(c) { return format!("{origin}{src}"); }
        }

**Last updated:** October 28, 2026

The **server-side / remote-projection HTML renderer**: a **stateless, streaming**
pure function of the opcode stream producing declarative HTML. Each render call
decodes a self-contained snapshot batch into a **transient** map, walks it once,
and emits HTML text out — no retained tree, zero cross-call state (Renderer
Statelessness). Protocol contract: `spec/`.

> **JVM note:** the Spring Boot / Quarkus paths no longer load this crate through
> JNA. `lib/java/pathland-render-html` is a **pure-Java behavioural port**, and
> `GoldenConformanceTest` keeps it byte-identical to this canonical renderer.

> source of the committed golden fixtures.

  (spec/PROXY.md §5). Without this arm the component fell to the `_ => String::new()`

- **Attributed text**: `SET_ATTRIBUTED_TEXT` decodes the binary payload into the
  node model and renders non-overlapping `<span style>` runs plus `<a href>`
  links (v1 attributes: font size/weight/color/style/design/underline/
  strikethrough); text and URLs are escaped, and the plain text remains the
  fallback. Covered by a unit test.

**Last updated:** October 28, 2026

The **server-side / remote-projection HTML renderer**: a **stateless, streaming**
pure function of the opcode stream producing declarative HTML. Each render call
decodes a self-contained snapshot batch into a **transient** map, walks it once,
and emits HTML text out — no retained tree, zero cross-call state (Renderer
Statelessness). Protocol contract: `spec/`.

> JNA. `lib/java/pathland-render-html` is a **pure-Java behavioural port**, and
> `GoldenConformanceTest` keeps it byte-identical to this canonical renderer.

> source of the committed golden fixtures.

  default and the spliced subtree was dropped. Covered by a unit test.

  node model and renders non-overlapping `<span style>` runs plus `<a href>`
  links (v1 attributes: font size/weight/color/style/design/underline/
  strikethrough); text and URLs are escaped, and the plain text remains the
  fallback. Covered by a unit test.

**Last updated:** November 6, 2026

The transport-agnostic Pathland server runtime: one app instance per session (SSR +
live 16-byte opcode deltas + environment), the session registry, and the **multi-app
host** (the BFF), shared by the Spring Boot and Quarkus starters. No web-framework
dependency — framework glue lives in the starters.

Rust all pass. `cargo fmt --check` failure is pre-existing due repo-wide unformatted files. Our changed files were formatted via cargo fmt -p earlier? `cargo fmt -p pathland-render-html` ran; `cargo fmt -p pathland-html-golden` ran. Good.

Now need ensure `pathland-ts-codegen` regenerated TS constants? We didn't change protocol constants, so no. But we added `pathland_render_html::DocumentMeta` - no generated output change. Fine.

Need maybe update `AGENTS.md`? Could mention but not necessary. However, AGENTS says status must update, done.

Now git diff review. Check for mistakes, especially PageMetadata docs, Rust structured data. Also check `document.rs` potential `image_url` returns `Some("")` if explicit empty? `image_url` meta.image_url clone; Java blankToNull. Fine.

Potential issue in Rust `structured_data.rs`: `find_paragraph` recursively calls and fallback at each level, so if a child returns none, fallback first body text of current node; maybe returns heading's sibling. Fine. But `find_paragraph` recurses and after recursion fallback; okay.

Potential issue in Rust `document::resolve`: window.title Some("") possible? WindowMeta clears empty to None, good. meta.title Some("") possible from builder with empty; then title empty. Java blankToNull -> null. Not identical for empty; we could make Rust builder blankToNull too for parity. Should we? `DocumentMeta.with_title("")` unlikely. But golden parity should hold for normal. Could normalize in `resolve`: `.filter(|s| !s.is_empty())`. Let's do to match Java and avoid empty title. Also image_url explicit empty should fall through. In `image_url`, meta.image_url.filter non-empty. Do. Also head_tags description empty: Java `description` may be null if blank; Rust could Some(""). Add filters. Let's improve parity:
```rust
let title = window.title.as_ref().filter(|s| !s.is_empty()).cloned()
 .or_else(|| meta.title.as_ref().filter(|s| !s.is_empty()).cloned())
 .unwrap_or...
let description = window.description.filter(non-empty).or(meta.description.filter(non-empty))
```
And image. Do.

Also Rust `DocumentMeta` fields public allow empty; resolve filters.

Let's patch.

state.output:
## Not implemented / gaps

- **`DESIGN_TOKEN` property references** cover the directly-mappable subset of
  the property catalog (colors, font size/weight/family, spacing/padding,
  corner radius, opacity, tint, border/shadow color, width/height). Compound
  accumulators that need concrete numbers (e.g. `BORDER_WIDTH`'s px suffix,
  shadow radius/x/y) remain literal-only.

- **Sequence gap detection** (`transport.ts`, spec/OPCODE.md §Sequence gap
  detection): each guest → host batch carries a per-stream monotonic `sequence`.
  The client baselines on the first batch and, when a batch's sequence breaks the
  chain (a batch was lost while the socket stayed open), **skips the gapped
  batch** and requests a full snapshot (`META::RESYNC`), then re-baselines.
  Host → guest heartbeat (`PONG`) batches are excluded; the baseline resets on
  every (re)connect. Tests cover contiguous runs (no resync), a gap (resync +
  skip), `PONG` exclusion, and re-baselining after a gap.
- **Grid/ScrollView/Lazy layout (spec/PRIMITIVES.md §Grid / §ScrollView)**:
  mirrors the Rust SSR — `grid-template-columns`/`grid-template-rows` from the
  `GRID_COLUMNS`/`GRID_ROWS` constructor properties (columns for GRID/
  LAZY_VGRID, rows for LAZY_HGRID + `grid-auto-flow:column`; never a pixel
  width/height), **`GRID_TRACKS`** per-track specs (`flex`/`fixed:<pts>`/
  `adaptive:<pts>` → `1fr`/`<pts>px`/`minmax(<pts>px,1fr)`, precedence over the
  count), `gap` from `SPACING`, greedy scroll
  (`flex:1 1 auto;align-self:stretch;overflow:auto`), and **per-cell grid
  alignment** — grid cells are wrapped in an auto-placed shell whose
  `justify-self`/`align-self` is `stretch` for a `FILL`/greedy cell else the
  grid `ALIGNMENT` position (`placedChild` + `applyLayout`, the ZStack mirror).
  **`GRID_ROW`** (0x1D) renders as a transparent `display:contents` element; its
  cell shells get explicit `grid-row`/`grid-column` placement (short rows leave
  trailing columns empty). `SCROLL` and `WHEEL` events are wired to
  document-level listeners gated by the listener bits. A runtime-inserted extra
  `SCROLLVIEW` child is a minor residual (SSR renders only the first child).
- **Canonical keyCode table**: `KEY_DOWN`/`KEY_UP` use the DOM `event.keyCode`
  convention; the renderer-shared canonical set lives in the conformance
  vectors (grant WP2) — cross-check on landing.
- **Visual tokens** (`PICKER_STYLE`, `CONTROL_SIZE`, `MINIMUM_SCALE_FACTOR`,
  `COLOR_MULTIPLY`) are applied as `data-*` attributes; their *visual* variety is
  renderer-styling-owned (Tailwind/theme), not the protocol's job.
- The element factory's runtime shells and the full property applier are
  golden-tested against the Rust SSR renderer via `test/ssr-conformance.test.ts`
  (fresh-DOM + hydrate-then-delta scenarios).
- `STATE`/`ROLE` map to ARIA attributes; exact bit semantics should be
  cross-checked against the conformance vectors when they land.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Multi-stage image for the Pathland Quarkus SSR demo (server-side HTML + /ws deltas).
# Build context is the repository root. The Java path is pure JVM (the HTML
# renderer is a Java port), so the image needs no Rust toolchain and the jar
# embeds no native library:
#
#   docker build -f lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/Dockerfile -t pathland-quarkus-demo .

# --- Stage 1: the Java reactor + the Quarkus app ---
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS java
WORKDIR /src
# The render-html module copies the generated base design from the Rust crate's
# committed assets; no Rust build is needed.
COPY lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets ./lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets
COPY lib/java ./lib/java
# Include the extension's deployment module in the reactor: the runtime module's
# quarkus-extension-maven-plugin validates its dependencies against it, and it is
# not a Maven dependency of the demo (so -am alone would omit it).
RUN mvn -q -B -f lib/java/pom.xml \
    -pl pathland-quarkus-demo,pathland-quarkus-deployment \
    -am package -Dmaven.test.skip=true

# --- Stage 2: runtime (JRE only) ---
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=java /src/lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/target/quarkus-app/ /app/
EXPOSE 8080
ENV QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT=8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-Xms64m", "-Xmx256m", "-jar", "/app/quarkus-run.jar"]

# Hardening Pathland deployments

Pathland has two distinct security surfaces:

1. **The protocol/client code** (`pathland-core`, `pathland-view-core`,
   `@pathland/dom-renderer`) — malformed opcodes must never panic, over-allocate,
   or execute markup/script. These bounds are fixed in code and covered by tests;
   reporting guidance lives in [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).
2. **The HTTP/WebSocket host** — origin checks, response headers, message-size
   limits, and rate limiting. These are framework/deployment concerns and are
   configured through Quarkus or Spring Boot.

This guide is Quarkus-first (the primary server target) with a Spring Boot
appendix.

## What Pathland does not use

- **No session cookie.** The per-window state scope (`wid`) lives in
  `sessionStorage` and is sent only on the WebSocket query string (and, when
  enabled, attached to navigations by the service worker). There is therefore no
  cookie to mark `HttpOnly`/`Secure`/`SameSite`.
- **No CSRF token.** SSR is read-only (`GET`), and the only state-changing
  channel is the WebSocket. WebSocket CSRF is prevented by the origin check
  below (browsers always send `Origin` on a WebSocket handshake).

## Quarkus (secure by default)

The `pathland-quarkus` extension contributes these runtime defaults via
`RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem`; application configuration always wins.

```properties
quarkus.http.cors.enabled=true
quarkus.websockets-next.server.max-message-size=65536
quarkus.websockets-next.server.max-frame-size=65536
quarkus.http.header."Content-Security-Policy".value=default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; media-src 'self'; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self' ws: wss:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; worker-src 'self'
quarkus.http.header."X-Content-Type-Options".value=nosniff
quarkus.http.header."Referrer-Policy".value=no-referrer
quarkus.http.header."X-Frame-Options".value=DENY
```

### WebSocket origin / CSRF

Quarkus's CORS filter runs before every route, including WebSocket upgrades.
With `cors.enabled=true` and **no `origins` configured**, it allows same-origin
requests only (missing `Origin` is allowed — non-browser clients). This is the
WebSocket CSRF control.

If browsers must connect from another origin, list them explicitly:

```properties
quarkus.http.cors.origins=https://app.example.com,https://staging.example.com
```

Never use `quarkus.http.cors.origins=*` for a stateful Pathland app. Quarkus has
one global CORS policy, so this also applies to non-WebSocket HTTP endpoints:
list any legitimate cross-origin API consumers, or set
`quarkus.http.cors.enabled=false` and enforce the origin check in your own
gateway/filter.

### CSP

The default policy allows same-origin scripts only. Inline **styles** are
unavoidable because the protocol emits `style` attributes and
`<style data-pathland-tokens>` / `data-pathland-fit` blocks, so `style-src`
includes `'unsafe-inline'`; scripts do not.

Override the policy (or relax it while rolling out) with application config:

```properties
quarkus.http.header."Content-Security-Policy".value=default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; ...
```

For an initial rollout you can use `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`
instead. Do not add `'unsafe-eval'` or `'unsafe-inline'` to `script-src`.

### Transport limits

- The extension pins WebSocket messages/frames to 64 KiB, matching the
  server-core inbound event-batch bound.
- Add a server-wide connection cap for a coarse DoS guard:

```properties
quarkus.http.limits.max-connections=1000
```

- Per-connection event batches and bytes are rate-limited in server-core
  (`pathland.max-inbound-batches-per-second`, default 500;
  `pathland.max-inbound-bytes-per-second`, default 2 MiB). Exceeding either
  drops the batch and increments `pathland.inbound.dropped`.
- For volumetric abuse, rate-limit at the edge (see below).

### Reverse proxy / TLS

Terminate TLS at the proxy and forward `X-Forwarded-Proto` / `X-Forwarded-Host`
(the same-origin check uses the request scheme + authority). Enable Quarkus's
proxy forwarding only when the proxy is trusted:

```properties
quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true
```

## Subresource Integrity

The SSR layer reads `dom-renderer.current`, which now has two lines:

```text
dom-renderer-<sha256-12>.js
sha384-<base64>
```

The script tag is emitted with `integrity="sha384-…"`. The bundle is same-origin,
content-hashed, and served `immutable`; SRI is defense-in-depth. If the second
line is absent (an older manifest), no `integrity` attribute is emitted.

Regenerate the bundle and manifests after a web-client change:

```bash
cd lib/typescript && npm run build:all
```

## Spring Boot appendix

The Spring Boot starter is supported, but Quarkus owns the secure defaults.
At minimum, set the WebSocket origin policy explicitly:

```properties
# Same-origin is the default when this is unset (Spring's handshake check).
# List explicit cross-origin hosts; never use '*'.
pathland.allowed-origins=https://app.example.com
```

Add CSP and the standard headers through Spring Security (or a small app-level
`OncePerRequestFilter`). Example security config:

```java
http.headers(headers -> headers
    .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives(
        "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; "
        + "img-src 'self' data:; media-src 'self'; font-src 'self'; "
        + "connect-src 'self' ws: wss:; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; "
        + "form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; worker-src 'self'"))
    .frameOptions(frame -> frame.deny())
    .referrerPolicy(referrer -> referrer.policy(
        org.springframework.security.web.header.writers.ReferrerPolicyHeaderWriter.ReferrerPolicy.NO_REFERRER))
    .contentTypeOptions(options -> {}));
```

Limit WebSocket payloads with a `ServletServerContainerFactoryBean`:

```java
@Bean
ServletServerContainerFactoryBean webSocketContainer() {
    var container = new ServletServerContainerFactoryBean();
    container.setMaxBinaryMessageBufferSize(64 * 1024);
    container.setMaxTextMessageBufferSize(64 * 1024);
    return container;
}
```

Configure Tomcat/server connection limits as needed (for example
`server.tomcat.max-connections`). Forwarded headers must be enabled when running
behind a proxy (`server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`).

## Edge rate limiting

The in-process limiter protects a single connection from flooding the session
actor. For volumetric or per-IP abuse, add a gateway/edge limit, for example:

```nginx
limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=pathland_ws:10m rate=10r/s;

location /_pathland/ws {
    limit_req zone=pathland_ws burst=20 nodelay;
    proxy_pass http://app;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
}
```

## Verification checklist

- `curl -I https://host/` → `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options`,
  `Referrer-Policy`, `X-Frame-Options`.
- SSR `<script>` carries `integrity="sha384-…"`.
- A WebSocket handshake with `Origin: https://evil.example` is rejected (403);
  same-origin succeeds.
- An event batch larger than 64 KiB is rejected without reaching the session.
- `pathland.inbound.dropped` stays at zero under normal interaction.

quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true

```
Maybe Render uses `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host` and Host may already be correct. Both configurations related to standard and non-standard headers can be combined, although the standard headers configuration will have precedence. However, combining them has security implications as clients can forge requests with a forwarded header that is not overwritten by the proxy. Therefore, proxies should strip unexpected `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-*` headers from the client.

By default, the `proto` values from `Forwarded` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers are validated against the URI scheme syntax. Requests with an invalid proto value receive a `400 Bad Request` response. Quarkus can be accessed through proxies that generate headers (e.g. `X-Forwarded-Host`) to preserve information about the original request. Quarkus can be configured to automatically update information like protocol, host, port and URI to use the values from those headers.

| Activating this feature can expose the server to security issues like information spoofing. Activate it only when running behind a reverse proxy. |
| --- |

To set up this feature for the management interface, include the following lines in `src/main/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.management.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true
```

To constrain this behavior to the standard `Forwarded` header (and ignore `X-Forwarded` variants) by setting `quarkus.management.proxy.allow-forwarded` in `src/main/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
quarkus.management.proxy.allow-forwarded=true
```

Alternatively, you can prefer `X-Forwarded-*` headers using the following configuration in `src/main/resources/application.properties` (note `allow-x-forwarded` instead of `allow-forwarded`):

```properties
quarkus.management.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true
quarkus.management.proxy.allow-x-forwarded=true
quarkus.management.proxy.enable-forwarded-host=true
quarkus.management.proxy.enable-forwarded-prefix=true
```

Supported forwarding address headers are:

- `Forwarded`
- `X-Forwarded-Proto`
- `X-Forwarded-Host`
- `X-Forwarded-Port`
- `X-Forwarded-Ssl`
- `X-Forwarded-Prefix`

If both header variants (`Forwarded` and `X-Forwarded-*`) are enabled, the `Forwarded` header will have precedence.

| Using both `Forwarded` and `X-Forwarded` headers can have security implications as it may allow clients to forge requests with a header that is not overwritten by the proxy. |
| --- |

Ensure that your proxy is configured to strip unexpected `Forwarded` or `X-Forwarded-*` headers from the client request.

Render forwards inbound requests to your web service at this port (it is not directly reachable via the public internet). We recommend binding your HTTP server to the port defined by the `PORT` environment variable. ## Diagnosis

The 403 is not a WebSocket bug — it is Quarkus’s **same-origin CORS/WebSocket CSRF check** working as designed, but seeing the wrong request origin.

Render terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to the container:

- Browser sends `Origin: https://pathland.onrender.com`
- Quarkus sees `http://<internal-host-or-:8080>` unless it trusts Render’s forwarded headers
- `CORSFilter.isSameOrigin` compares scheme first, so `https` vs `http` fails → **403**

The same issue also makes the new SSR canonical URL use the internal `http://…` origin. Fixing proxy trust fixes both.

## Plan

### 1. Enable forwarded headers in the Quarkus demo

Add to `lib/java/pathland-quarkus-demo/src/main/resources/application.properties`:

```properties
# Render (and any TLS-terminating reverse proxy) forwards the external
# scheme/host. Without this, Quarkus sees http://<internal-host> while the
# browser Origin is https://pathland.onrender.com → CORS/WebSocket 403.
quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true
quarkus.http.proxy.allow-x-forwarded=true
quarkus.http.proxy.enable-forwarded-host=true
```

This keeps same-origin enforcement intact; it just compares against the real external origin.

### 2. Optional immediate workaround

Set these Render environment variables now, before redeploying code:

```text
QUARKUS_HTTP_PROXY_PROXY_ADDRESS_FORWARDING=true
QUARKUS_HTTP_PROXY_ALLOW_X_FORWARDED=true
QUARKUS_HTTP_PROXY_ENABLE_FORWARDED_HOST=true
```

### 3. Update hardening docs

In `docs/HARDENING.md` → “Reverse proxy / TLS”, document all three keys (it currently mentions only `proxy-address-forwarding`) and explain that Render/Vercel/Fly-style TLS terminators require `enable-forwarded-host` for the canonical URL and same-origin WebSocket check.

### 4. Add a regression test

Add a Quarkus demo test (or extend `SeoHeadTest`) that sends:

```http
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Host: example.com
Origin: https://example.com
```

and asserts:

- SSR returns 200 (same-origin accepted)
- canonical is `https://example.com/...` (not `http://...`)

Optionally extend `WsSession` with an extra-header overload so a real WebSocket handshake can be tested with forwarded headers too.

### 5. Verify

- `cd lib/java && mvn -pl pathland-quarkus-demo -am test`
- Full `mvn install`
- After redeploy: browser WebSocket returns `101 Switching Protocols`, no reconnect loop, and `curl`/view-source shows an `https://pathland.onrender.com/...` canonical URL.

No protocol, renderer, or DOM-client changes are needed.

parts.text:
We need propose a plan that changes defaults so hosted works out of the box. We can consider enabling proxy forwarding by default in security defaults. But user specifically says "default security should not require the developer to specify these headers in order to run it in a hosted setup. We do want to inform them about how to make it secure, but it must be easy first and foremost and then secure."

This suggests:
- Set sensible defaults that work on hosted platforms.
- Document security implications and how to tighten.
- Perhaps make "trust forwarded headers" default only for scheme/host (which are needed) and not for remote IP? Quarkus setting controls all. Could set `proxy-address-forwarding=true` by default; document direct exposure caveat.

But maybe instead of trusting headers, we can make the default origin check independent of scheme/host mismatch by using `quarkus.http.cors.origins`? No dynamic. Or configure CORS `origins` with a regex matching any host? That would defeat CSRF.

Could use Quarkus's `quarkus.http.cors.origins` from an env var? Not default.

Could change the DOM client's WebSocket URL to use an origin that matches server scheme? Browser always uses wss for https page. Cannot.

Thus default proxy forwarding is likely the practical route. Need decide scope:
- Quarkus extension default set `quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=true`, `allow-x-forwarded=true`, `enable-forwarded-host=true`.
- But what about direct deployments (e.g., `java -jar` on a VPS)? Trusting forwarded headers by default means clients can spoof scheme/host; for same-origin, browser can't set these headers. For SSR canonical, a client can make their own response canonical point elsewhere; no shared cache typically. Could be exploited for cache poisoning if CDN caches without Vary on forwarded headers; edge would strip. Acceptable with docs.
- Still retain explicit CORS same-origin. Good.

Alternative default: `proxy-address-forwarding=true` but `enable-forwarded-host=false` (use Host header) and only scheme forwarded. Render's Host is maybe internal; canonical would be https://internalhost. That would fail SEO canonical and maybe origin host comparison if Host internal. So enable forwarded host too.
- `allow-x-forwarded=true` explicit.

Then docs:
- New section "Hosted/PaaS deployments (works by default)" explaining defaults trust `X-Forwarded-*` so hosted platforms work without config.
- "Directly internet-facing deployments" explain set `quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=false` or restrict `quarkus.http.proxy.trusted-proxies`/strip headers.
- Update verification checklist.

What about Spring Boot default? The Spring starter's WebSocket origin check uses Spring's `WebUtils.isSameOrigin(headers)` which checks `Origin` against `Host`/`X-Forwarded-*` using `ForwardedHeaderFilter` only if configured. We could similarly make Spring easy:
- Set `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` by default via auto-configuration. How? In Spring Boot, `server.forward-headers-strategy` is read by `ForwardedHeaderFilter` auto-config? It's a property in `ServerProperties` enumerated at auto-config. If we set a default via `EnvironmentPostProcessor` or a property source, could force framework. But we shouldn't override user explicit config. Could register a `ForwardedHeaderFilter` bean unconditionally? That would honor headers always, even if direct. Same tradeoff.
- Or add a custom `WebSocketHandler` origin check that uses forwarded headers. But current uses Spring's default.
- Maybe the user only cares about Quarkus/Render now, but they said "default security" generally. Plan should include Spring parity: add `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` as a default via `EnvironmentPostProcessor` (or `@Bean` filter) and document opt-out. But changing Spring default globally may be broader.

Let's inspect Spring auto config current WebSocket registration and origin. It sets `setAllowedOrigins` if configured, otherwise Spring's default same-origin check. Spring Boot's `ForwardedHeaderFilter` only installed when `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`. There is also `Native` strategy on Tomcat: `RemoteIpValve` which honors X-Forwarded-* by default if present. `server.forward-headers-strategy` default is `NATIVE`? Let me recall Spring Boot 3: default `NATIVE`? Documented: "NATIVE: Use native support for forwarded headers if available; FRAMEWORK: use ForwardedHeaderFilter; NONE: disable." Default is `NATIVE`? Actually `ServerProperties.ForwardHeadersStrategy` default null; `ForwardedHeaderFilter` auto-config sets default based on `CloudPlatform` (if cloud platform -> NATIVE else NONE). On Render not detected -> NONE. Tomcat's RemoteIpValve can be enabled via `server.tomcat.remoteip.remote-ip-header=x-forwarded-for` or `server.forward-headers-strategy=native` maybe. So Spring hosted may also fail.

We can propose:
- Provide default behavior at the starter level: register a `ForwardedHeaderFilter` (framework strategy) in both starters? For Spring, add a `FilterRegistrationBean<ForwardedHeaderFilter>` with order highest, or an `EnvironmentPostProcessor` setting `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework` if unset. The latter respects explicit user config. But does Quarkus extension default similarly.
- For direct exposure, docs advise disabling.

However, maybe better to not change actual security defaults in framework, but make the demo/deployment easy via environment variables? User explicitly rejects requiring developer to specify. So defaults.

Could also make `pathland-quarkus` not enable CORS by default (remove `quarkus.http.cors.enabled=true`) and instead rely on WebSocket origin check? Then no 403 on WS? Wait Quarkus WebSocket Next may have its own origin check? The 403 is CORS filter. If we disable CORS, WS handshake may succeed but then we lose CSRF. Could implement our own check using Origin host + Host/X-Forwarded-Host with scheme-agnostic? That would be "easy and secure". Maybe that's the ideal architectural solution:

- Keep same-origin enforcement, but compare only authority, not scheme, when behind a proxy? We can't know. But accepting either http/https for matching host is a small relaxation. Is it secure enough? Origin scheme mismatch should only occur behind TLS terminator; direct clients cannot fake Origin (browser sets it). If site is served over both http and https, same host, cross-scheme CSRF already possible; HSTS mitigates. SameSite cookies not used. Since no cookies are used, WebSocket CSRF only matters if a malicious page can connect to same host with victim's network credentials. If attacker can host page on `http://example.com`, they already control the host. So scheme-agnostic same-host check is reasonable.
- Then we could avoid trusting X-Forwarded-* for scheme; use Host header for authority and accept scheme either http/https. But if Host header is internal (Render may preserve public Host; likely yes) then host mismatch. We can also check X-Forwarded-Host as an alternate candidate. That's trusting forwarded host only for origin match; safe-ish.
- Implementing our own filter for both Quarkus WS and HTTP plus Spring is more code and duplicates framework. But maybe less config and no broad proxy trust.

Yet the canonical URL still needs external scheme/host; for that we'd still need forwarded headers to render correct SEO. We could limit trust to building canonical URL by reading X-Forwarded-Proto/Host directly in `IndexResource`/Spring controller, not globally enabling proxy forwarding. But then Origin check? Could implement origin validation ourselves. More work but secure/easy.

But is that overkill? The user's priority "easy first and foremost and then secure"—perhaps they prefer enabling proxy defaults. The phrase "We do want to inform them about how to make it secure" suggests default could be easy (trust forwarded headers) and docs explain hardening for direct exposure. I think that's the intended direction.

Let's propose a nuanced default:
- **Default: hosted-friendly.** Enable forwarded-header handling in the extension/starters, so TLS-terminating platforms work with zero config. Keep same-origin CORS and CSP.
- **Documented hardening:** For directly exposed deployments, either:
  - disable forwarded headers (`quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=false` / Spring `server.forward-headers-strategy=none`), or
  - restrict to trusted proxy IPs (`quarkus.http.proxy.trusted-proxies=...`), or
  - strip `X-Forwarded-*` at the edge.
- Maybe use `trusted-proxies` default? Quarkus defaults all proxies trusted. Could set docs.

But is enabling forwarded headers in the extension "default security" change acceptable given issue #63? The user explicitly asks. We need also consider tests:
- Quarkus: `securityDefaults()` add three keys. Update `PathlandProcessor` tests? Are there tests asserting defaults? Search.

Alternative for Spring: register a custom WebSocket `HandshakeInterceptor` that compares origin host with request host plus forwarded host and ignores scheme mismatch. But then HTTP CORS? There is no CORS filter in Spring by default; SSG page same-origin. The only security check is WebSocket. So we can make the Spring WS origin check hosted-friendly without globally enabling forwarded headers:
- Replace/augment default Spring same-origin check with `PathlandOriginCheck` that:
  - if `pathland.allowed-origins` configured, use those.
  - else accept if Origin missing, or Origin host equals one of `Host`/`X-Forwarded-Host`, regardless of scheme.
  - This works behind proxies and direct.
- But canonical URL in Spring still uses `request.getRequestURL()`, would show http://internal unless forwarded strategy. So need forwarded headers for canonical too. Could build canonical from `Forwarded`/`X-Forwarded-*` directly in controller with fallback. But that's another path. Maybe easier to enable framework forwarded headers.

Given user asks general "hosted setup", I think enabling forwarded headers defaults in both is acceptable and simplest. Need be transparent in plan about security tradeoff and opt-outs.

However, perhaps we can scope defaults to known PaaS via detection? Spring has `CloudPlatform` detection only for CF/Heroku/Kubernetes; not Render. Quarkus no. Could detect `RENDER` env var? Too platform-specific.

Another thought: Instead of trusting forwarded headers, set CORS default to **allow same host regardless of scheme**. Quarkus doesn't support that. Spring could custom. Quarkus could use `quarkus.http.cors.origins` regex? The allowed origin regex matches full origin string; could set a regex that matches any `https?://...`? That would allow all origins, defeating CSRF. Could set regex that matches `https?://` + host? Host is dynamic, not available in regex. No.

Could we use `quarkus.http.cors.origins` with `https://*`? That's wildcard? Not host-specific.

Could disable CORS and implement our own. Too much.

Maybe the best plan, balancing: 
- **Default to trusting forwarded headers** in Quarkus extension (and Spring starter) because hosted is the common path; this only affects scheme/host/client-IP derivation.
- Keep same-origin and CSP enforcement.
- Document opt-out/hardening clearly.
- Add tests for forwarded scheme/host (SSR canonical + WS handshake).

## Revised direction

The previous plan put the burden on the app/deployment. Instead, the framework defaults should make a normal hosted deployment work with **zero configuration**, while `docs/HARDENING.md` explains how to tighten them for directly exposed deployments.

Root cause remains: Render terminates TLS and forwards HTTP with `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` / `X-Forwarded-Host`, but Quarkus compares the browser’s `https://…` origin against the internal `http://…` request. Fixing the default forwarded-header handling also fixes the SSR canonical URL.

## Plan

### 1. Quarkus extension: hosted-friendly defaults

In `lib/java/pathland-quarkus-deployment/src/main/java/dev/pathland/quarkus/deployment/PathlandProcessor.java`, add to the existing `securityDefaults()`:

```java
new RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem(
        "quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding", "true"),
new RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem(
        "quarkus.http.proxy.allow-x-forwarded", "true"),
new RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem(
        "quarkus.http.proxy.enable-forwarded-host", "true"),
```

This makes Render/Fly/Heroku/Cloud Run-style deployments work out of the box:

- WebSocket same-origin check sees `https://pathland.onrender.com` instead of `http://<internal-host>`.
- SSR canonical/OG URLs use the public HTTPS origin.
- Same-origin CORS/CSRF enforcement remains in place.

Application config still wins, so a direct-exposure deployment can set `quarkus.http.proxy.proxy-address-forwarding=false`.

### 2. Spring Boot starter: parity by default

Make the Spring starter honor forwarded headers without requiring `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`:

- Add an `EnvironmentPostProcessor` in `pathland-spring-boot-starter` that contributes a **lowest-precedence** default:
  ```properties
  server.forward-headers-strategy=framework
  ```
- Register it via `META-INF/spring.factories`.
- Because it is lowest precedence, an explicit `server.forward-headers-strategy=native|none` still wins.
- This makes `request.getRequestURL()` (canonical URL) and Spring’s WebSocket same-origin check use the external scheme/host.

If we prefer not to add an EPP, the fallback is a `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` `ForwardedHeaderFilter` bean plus a `pathland.forwarded-headers` opt-out, but the standard Spring property is cleaner and more predictable.

### 3. Do not add per-demo headers

Remove the idea of adding `quarkus.http.proxy.*` to `pathland-quarkus-demo/application.properties`. The starter defaults are the contract; demos and apps inherit them.

### 4. Documentation: easy by default, hardening explained

- Add a **“Hosted deployments (default)”** section explaining that forwarded headers are trusted by default so PaaS/TLS-terminating setups work with no config.

**Spring Boot (current code):** Pathland reads values with `@Value("${property:default}")`, so an explicit application property already wins.

**Spring Boot (proposed forwarded-header default):** it must be implemented as a **lowest-precedence property source**, not an unconditional filter bean or programmatic setter. Then an explicit:

```properties
server.forward-headers-strategy=native
# or
server.forward-headers-strategy=none
```

still wins.

## The real caveat

If an existing app never set one of these keys, adding Pathland introduces a behavior change because Pathland supplies a default:

- CORS becomes enabled
- forwarded headers become trusted
- WebSocket message caps are set
- CSP / `X-Frame-Options` / etc. headers are added
- WebSocket connections may start using an external scheme/host

That is a **default**, not an override — but it is still a behavior change for an app that relied on “unset”. It should be documented clearly, with one-line opt-outs.

Also note a separate risk: if the app already adds security headers through its own filter, Pathland’s default `quarkus.http.header.*` values do not override them, but could produce **duplicate headers**. Not a config override, but worth documenting.

## Plan additions

1. **Contract:** Pathland only supplies framework defaults; it never mutates app configuration programmatically, never calls setters that bypass config, and never registers an unconditional bean that ignores the standard property.

2. **Add override regression tests:**
   - Quarkus test app explicitly sets all Pathland default keys (`cors.enabled`, proxy forwarding, header values, WebSocket limits) to custom values; assert the app values survive.
   - Spring test explicitly sets `server.forward-headers-strategy=none` and a custom CSP; assert Pathland does not force forwarding and does not replace the app CSP.

3. **Docs:** add a “Pathland defaults never override your configuration” section with:
   - A precedence table (system > env > profile > application.properties > Pathland default).
   - A list of exactly which defaults Pathland contributes and what changes if they were previously unset.
   - One-line opt-outs for each behavior.

4. **Spring implementation choice** (needs your preference):
   - **Option A (recommended):** lowest-precedence `EnvironmentPostProcessor` setting `server.forward-headers-strategy=framework`. Consistent with Quarkus, zero-config, and explicit app config wins.
   - **Option B:** Pathland-only forwarded handling — a custom WebSocket handshake interceptor plus a canonical-URL helper that reads forwarded headers only for Pathland endpoints. Narrowest blast radius, but duplicates origin/canonical logic and does not change global Spring behavior.

Which Spring approach do you prefer for the implementation plan?

+  correct WebSocket same-origin check and external SSR canonical URL with zero
+  configuration. An explicit `server.forward-headers-strategy` in application
+  config always wins (`ForwardedHeaderOverrideTest` pins this).
 - **Java host / Kotlin views**: `KotlinViewMountTest` proves a Java-only
   `@SpringBootApplication` bean returning `PathlandApp` mounts a Kotlin-authored
   fixture view, renders it through SSR, and receives a live signal delta.
 
 - **Crawler endpoints**: `/robots.txt` (text/plain) and `/sitemap.xml` (application/xml) are real routes before the SPA catch-all, so Lighthouse does not parse the HTML shell as robots.txt.
 - **SEO document head (issue #45)**: the SSR controller derives the canonical
   URL from the request and passes host-default `PageMetadata` to the registry;
   `PathlandApp.pageMetadata(...)` may override it per route before the first
   paint. Canonical/OG/Twitter/JSON-LD are on by default and configurable via
   `pathland.seo.{enabled,site-name,image,og-type,twitter-card,twitter-site,structured-data}`.
 
 - **`PathlandAutoConfiguration`** (`@AutoConfiguration`, `@EnableWebSocket` since Spring
   Boot 3.5 no longer auto-enables it) + `META-INF/spring/…/AutoConfiguration.imports`:
   - default `StateStore` bean (`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — Redis-or-in-memory),
   - `PathlandHost` bean (shut down with the context): every `MountedApp` bean plus the
     lone `PathlandApp` bean mounted at `/` (unless an explicit `MountedApp` claims the
     root). Without any app the host is empty and the starter is inert.
   - a `WebSocketConfigurer` registering **one handler per app** at its framework base
     (`/_pathland/ws` for the root, `/{mount}/_pathland/ws` otherwise). Each connection
     gets a fresh `uiId` (its UI model) + the client's `wid` (per-window state scope)
     from the WS `?wid=` query param (kept in `sessionStorage`, never in the page URL),
   - `PathlandIndexController` (SSR catch-all dispatching to the longest-mount app with
     the prefix stripped + a framework static controller serving the bundle + asset mount
     from `classpath:/static/_pathland/**` at both `/_pathland/**` and `/{app}/_pathland/**`;
     the more-specific mapping beats `/{*path}`, and the `!Upgrade` header excludes WS).
     When no static file matches, the controller serves renderer-owned assets from the
     shared Rust renderer: the content-hashed base stylesheet
     (`HtmlRenderer.baseCss()` at `baseCssName()`) as `text/css` with
     `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, and
     `/_pathland/icons/{name}.svg` glyphs (`HtmlRenderer.iconSvg` →
     `pathland_html_icon_svg`) with an `immutable` cache header — no static CSS/icon
     files on any host, and a host can still override either with a file. SSR links
     the CSS via `PathlandSession` → `renderLinked`.
     The framework controller honors byte-range requests (`206 Partial Content` +
     `Content-Range`, `416` for unsatisfiable ranges, `Accept-Ranges` on the full
     response) — a `<video>` (a `MediaController`'s playback) seeking beyond its
     buffer issues a `Range`
     request, and answering it with a full `200` would make browsers restart the media
     at byte 0.
     SSR renders defaults (no session cookie — per-window state arrives over the WS).
 - **SSR debug comments**: the host reads the `pathland.debug-html` property
   (`@Value("${pathland.debug-html:false}")`) and forwards it to each registry, enabling
   per-node HTML comments in SSR output when set.
 - **Per-window-id service worker (opt-in, issue #155)**: `pathland.service-worker`
   (default `false`) forwards to the host; the SSR emits `data-pathland-service-worker`
   and the controller serves `{base}/sw.js` with `Service-Worker-Allowed: /` +
   `Cache-Control: no-cache` (a stable, uncached script the browser byte-compares).
 - **`SpringConnection`** — adapts `WebSocketSession` to `PathlandConnection`.
   `AutoCloseable`: a failed send surfaces as a close (the session's
   `closeConnection` closes the underlying session) so the DOM client reconnects +
   `META::RESYNC` instead of silently stalling on an open socket.
 - **Heartbeat** — the socket replies to a client `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
   **at the transport layer** (through its `SpringConnection`, no actor/session
   dependency; spec/OPCODE.md §Transport heartbeat).
 - **Observability (issue #62)** — `spring-boot-starter-actuator` supplies the
   `MeterRegistry`; auto-config builds a `MicrometerTelemetry` over it (decorated with
   `TracingTelemetry` when an `OpenTelemetry` bean is present — add
   `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel` to opt in) and a `HealthIndicator` reporting the host
   UP with `activeSessions`/`mounts` at `/actuator/health`. The `pathland.*` meters are
   exposed at `/actuator/prometheus` (add `micrometer-registry-prometheus`).
 
 ## App DX
 
 ```java
 @SpringBootApplication
 public class MyApp {
     public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); }
     @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); }
     @Bean MountedApp support() { return MountedApp.of("/support", ...); } // optional 2nd app
 }
 ```
 
 ## Verified by
 
 `mvn test` — `PathlandAutoConfigurationTest` (`@SpringBootTest`): a `PathlandApp` bean
 mounts at `/` and SSR renders the root. `MultiSessionWebSocketTest`
 (`@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT)`) opens **100 concurrent real WS sessions** against
 `/_pathland/ws` (via the shared `pathland-server-core` test-jar probe) and asserts each
 connects, re-syncs, gets transport-level PONGs, stays isolated, and is never closed by
 the peer. `PathlandObservabilityTest` (`@SpringBootTest` + `MockMvc`) asserts
 `/actuator/health` reports the `pathland` component UP and the auto-configured
 `PathlandTelemetry` is a `MicrometerTelemetry` registering `pathland.*` meters.
 `BaseCssHeadersTest` (`@SpringBootTest` + `MockMvc`) asserts the linked SSR
 `<link>`, the immutable `text/css` response at the global and mounted bases, and
 a 404 for an unknown hash.
 Manual: the `pathland-spring-boot-demo` renders `/`, `/kitchen`, `/settings`
 and the 404 fallback **and a second app at `/app2`**; a WebSocket handshake to
 `/_pathland/ws` and `/app2/_pathland/ws` returns 101.
\ No newline at end of file

Spring Boot's `ConfigDataEnvironmentPostProcessor` order is `Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10`? Let's verify. If ours is LOWEST_PRECEDENCE, runs last, after application config loaded. `addLast` then lowest. Good.

But `withDefaultValues` is in generated config builder; should be global. Yet `@ConfigProperty` lookup during runtime after config built should see. Unless `@ConfigProperty` uses a different Config instance? Hmm.

Maybe the default build item is overwritten by another extension default for same key with `false`—e.g., some other extension or Quarkus itself sets default false via `RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem`. Built-in `@WithDefault("false")` is not a build item, though. Maybe `quarkus-kubernetes` or another extension? Unlikely.

  `sessionStorage` and is sent only on the WebSocket query string (and, when

  cookie to mark `HttpOnly`/`Secure`/`SameSite`.

  channel is the WebSocket. WebSocket CSRF is prevented by the origin check

`RunTimeConfigurationDefaultBuildItem`; application configuration always wins.

quarkus.http.header."X-Content-Type-Options".value=nosniff
quarkus.http.header."Referrer-Policy".value=no-referrer
quarkus.http.header."X-Frame-Options".value=DENY

We set `proxyForwarding` default true annotation; if extension default disabled by app false, works. Potential issue: Quarkus manual canonical path uses `uri.getRequestUri().getRawPath()` only, not query; good. If `X-Forwarded-Prefix` used, not handled; not needed.
